item.title: Inside the Plague Research Labs at the Heart of a Russian Mystery
item.description: A Russian researcher, who died from an unknown illness, worked at a remote anti-plague facility. Few foreigners have visited these labs, which dot the former Soviet states, and are shrouded in secrecy.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute, via Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A picture released by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute showing specialists working in a laboratory in Krasnoyarsk, Russia, in 2019.

item.title: A New World of Lung Cancer Therapy Awaits Pope Leo
item.description: Lung cancer is still a leading cause of cancer death, but that rate is half what it was in the 1990s, partly because newly developed treatments are working.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata and Carolyn Y. Johnson
item.media:description: Pope Leo greeted his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, as he arrived at the Gemelli Hospital in Rome on Tuesday to remove a lung nodule.

item.title: They Created a Cell That’s Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now?
item.description: SpudCells may one day produce new medicines and materials. But first scientists have to improve them — and make sure they aren’t misused.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: How Top Trump Officials Stoked Fears of a Nuke That Could Fry the Power Grid
item.description: For more than a decade, conservative activists held that a single atomic bomb could, without killing Americans directly, lay waste to the country — a claim that built fervor for war with Iran.
item.dc:creator: William J. Broad
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:description: The test detonation in 1962 of a hydrogen bomb lit up the night sky over Honolulu and knocked out some of the city’s electrical systems. Experts linked the unanticipated damage to what they came to call the electromagnetic pulse.

item.title: What Can Four-Winged Dinosaurs Teach Us About Birds?
item.description: Flight was probably more widespread in dinosaurs than previously thought. A newly identified species sheds light on how some achieved liftoff.
item.dc:creator: Jack Tamisiea

item.title: There’s Worlds Out There More Habitable Than Earth
item.description: Scientists believe there are planets outside our solar system where life is even more abundant and sustainable.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Wolchover

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Rover Sets a Mars Driving Record
item.description: Advances in self-driving technology have made it easier to traverse distant worlds.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: How Do Cuttlefish Hide? Scientists Search for the Secret to Camouflage.
item.description: Cephalopods are masters of camouflage. Scientists want to decipher how the process works in the brain.
item.dc:creator: Alexa Robles-Gil

item.title: Who Were the Vikings? 21 Graves Weave a Tale of Hunters, Nomads and Sorceresses.
item.description: “The Sea-King and the Sorceress” examines the lives and deaths of the diverse people who called themselves Vikings.
item.dc:creator: Franz Lidz
item.category: The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age (Book)

item.title: Bleached Coral Rebounded After Touching Healthy Coral, Study Finds
item.description: After sick corals were placed in direct contact with healthy ones of the same genetic make-up, they recovered at “incredible” speed, scientists found.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong

item.title: Amit Forlit, the Israeli Private Eye at the Heart of a Climate Hacking Scandal
item.description: He’s been linked to someone called “The Hawk.” He named his company “This Isn’t a Dentist’s Office.” The feds say he hacked American environmentalists.
item.dc:creator: Karen Zraick and Gabby Sobelman

item.title: How a Logging Industry Downturn Fuels Wildfires
item.description: Loggers are finding it impossible to profitably harvest some federal forests. That leaves more fuel for fires to accumulate.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:description: The Plaskett Fire burning in California in August.

item.title: He Helped Discover Ebola 50 Years Ago. He’s Still Worried.
item.description: In an interview, Dr. Peter Piot recalled when he first saw the spindly virus under a microscope and reflected on a five-decade career spent fighting two deadly pathogens.
item.dc:creator: Apoorva Mandavilli
item.media:description: Dr. Peter Piot was among the first scientists to see the Ebola virus, as a young researcher in Belgium in 1976.

item.title: The Times’s New Space Editor Has Her Eye on the Cosmos
item.description: On the Science desk, Victoria Jaggard spends her days pondering the universe’s most pressing mysteries.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Bahr

item.title: New York City’s Latest Famous Family Is a Hoot. Yes, They’re Barn Owls.
item.description: The city’s latest feathered extraordinaires are captivating the Upper West Side with their screeches.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Maag
item.media:description: Barn owls are rarely seen in dense urban areas like New York City.

item.title: Why Ketamine Immobilizes Some Users
item.description: Potent powders can produce a nearly catatonic state, particularly in those who have not tried the drug before.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Jacobs
item.media:credit: Sandy Huffaker for The New York Times
item.media:description: Ketamine is a useful sedative and antidepressant at light doses. At stronger doses, it is a powerful anesthetic, but at repeated high doses, it deadens sensation, leaving users conscious but unable to act.

item.title: Mathematician Who Waited 50 Years for Proper Credit for Her Work Has Died
item.description: At the Los Alamos National Laboratory, Mary Tsingou Menzel’s computer programming helped set the stage for chaos theory and other fields.
item.dc:creator: Ama Sarpomaa

item.title: Will We Ever Understand Dementia?
item.description: Since the days of Dr. Alzheimer himself, there has been a dream that severe senility might have an explanation — and a cure. The search for both has never been more urgent.
item.dc:creator: Robert Kolker
item.media:credit: Oliver Farshi for The New York Times

item.title: The Underappreciated Benefits of Leaving Fallen Leaves Alone
item.description: To homeowners, fallen leaves look like work. To nature, they’re an investment, with tremendous value on the secondary market as invertebrate real estate.
item.dc:creator: Alan Burdick

item.title: Big Controversy Upends a Contest About Microscopic Videos
item.description: Nikon announced that it had disqualified the winner of its Small World in Motion competition over how A.I. was used in his submission.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu
item.media:description: Nikon’s Small World in Motion competition is an annual video contest that awards the best footage captured through the lens of a microscope.

item.title: Cancer Vaccines Are the N.I.H.’s Next ‘Big Bet’
item.description: New details have emerged about an initiative that starts in December to fast-track the vaccines, similar to the successful push for the Covid-19 vaccine.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:description: Cancer vaccine research at the biotech company Moderna in Cambridge, Mass., which reported in August promising results that a melanoma vaccine increased the time before cancers recurred and increased the time before the cancers spread.

item.title: What Are the Remaining Millennium Prize Problems?
item.description: OpenAI’s trove of new math results doesn’t fully solve any of these highly prestigious open questions, but it seems to make progress on some.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:description: A page from an 1859 manuscript in which Berhard Reimann formulated his famous hypothesis, one of the remaining Millennium Prize problems.

item.title: ‘Breathtaking,’ ‘Devastating’: Mathematics Reels After New OpenAI Release
item.description: Hundreds of new A.I.-generated findings moved the frontiers of higher math in a single day — dispelling any doubt that the field is forever changed.
item.dc:creator: Siobhan Roberts
item.media:credit: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times
item.media:description: Experts say the cataclysmic upheaval to the field will affect students the most, especially graduate students on the cusp of becoming a part of this intellectual community.

item.title: 21 Birds Are Found at Miami Airport Stuffed in Underwear and Hidden in a Belt
item.description: Two men, who arrived separately from Cuba days apart, each carried clutches of live birds concealed in their clothes, the authorities said.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Chao
item.media:description: A man who was detained at Miami International Airport on Sunday appeared nervous and had an “unexplained bulge” around his pelvis, according to a criminal complaint.

item.title: The National Hurricane Center’s Boss Keeps an Eye on the Storms
item.description: The director, Michael Brennan, oversees 45 federal workers, including hurricane specialists and meteorologists.
item.dc:creator: Johnny Diaz
item.media:description: Michael Brennan has been director of the National Hurricane Center since 2023.

item.title: Before Computer Science Became a Boys’ Club, Margaret Hamilton Wrote the Code
item.description: The woman who helped put astronauts on the moon was a software engineer when the field was not prestigious or lucrative.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson and Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, via Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: As Flood Risk Increases in Himalayas, Nepal Builds More in Vulnerable Areas
item.description: The total footprint of buildings along flood-prone riverbanks in the Himalayas grew by half in recent years, a study found.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
item.media:credit: Jason Gulley for The New York Times
item.media:description: Flood hazards in Nepal include monsoon downpours, earthquakes and avalanches that send boulders tumbling into lakes formed by melting glaciers.

item.title: For Two Sisters, a “Biological Age Test” Measured More Than Their DNA
item.description: They thought it might explain why their health had diverged. Instead, it stirred up feelings that weren’t so easily quantified.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn and Annie Flanagan
item.media:credit: Vivian Dehning; photographs by Annie Flanagan for The New York Times
